item.title: Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant political development with concrete details and useful vocabulary.

Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says

Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart has said his party would scrap the deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday, if the Tories win the next general election.

The agreement signed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham covers a youth travel scheme, emissions trading and British food exports.

The government has argued scrapping most checks on British food exports will cut costs for businesses and could bring down prices for shoppers.

Burghart told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme the deal was "a dog's dinner", which would not lead to lower prices in the shops and would mean the UK "gives up our ability to set our own rules".

Under the agreement, the UK will also have to follow some EU regulations.

Burghart acknowledged the deal would reduce some trade "friction" but he said it would put a "massive additional burden on the 90% of farmers that don't do any trade with the EU".

Pressed over whether the Conservatives were committed to scrapping the deal if the party wins the next general election, Burghart said: "I don't think that there will be positive outcomes, and yes, we would scrap it."

He added: "I also don't think it is a good idea for a country like Britain to hand over control of its rules to another power and have no say over how those rules are created right into the future."

Food retailers have welcomed the deal, saying it will cut costs, reduce bureaucracy and remove barriers to trade.

However, they have not committed to cutting prices as a direct result of the changes.

The British Retail Consortium has said it does not expect prices on supermarket shelves to fall in response to the deal.

It has said upward pressures on prices remain and will not be alleviated by the agreement.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband insisted the deal "reduces pressure on trading costs", adding: "They're the things that go into prices."

"It will reduce the costs that the retailers face, all of that Brexit red tape, millions of forms that they were having to fill in, frankly pointlessly, as a result of the bad deal that we had," he told the BBC.

Challenged that the UK was also giving up some powers to set regulations itself, Miliband argued businesses were already "rule takers" from Brussels if they wanted to sell into the European market.

"So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union. But at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms... to confirm that they're observing the right standards, which is frankly crackers," he said.

Under the deal, he said the UK would "be able to shape decisions" for the first time.

Reform UK has also criticised the UK-EU deal.

Deputy leader Richard Tice told Sky News that while "a few exporting food businesses may benefit", companies that do not export to the EU will still have to align with EU rules.

"Divergence is now our strength. We need to be scrapping net zero so we can bring down energy bills, whereas the EU is still ideologically obsessed with it," he said

"The extra burdens of EU regulations that will be forced through dynamic alignment across all UK businesses is way more than that small net benefit."

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week, with the food exports deal in force from 2028.

Elsewhere in the agreement, a new "youth experience scheme" will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the EU for up to three years.

The same number of young people from the EU will also be allowed into the UK.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A proposal from the bloc to lower the level of university tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed and talks on this aspect will continue. Miliband has said Friday's deal is not dependent on an agreement on tuition fees.

The Conservatives have also criticised the youth experience scheme, saying people from the EU will be competing with young Britons struggling to get jobs.

The Liberal Democrats have welcomed the scheme as "a big step forward" but have said "it's nowhere near enough".

The party has called for the UK to rejoin the EU single market and customs union to help cut the cost of living and grow the economy.

item.title: Closer EU ties will give UK say on Brussels decisions, says Ed Miliband
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains the potential benefits of closer EU ties with clear prose and useful context.

Closer links with the EU will mean the UK having a say on decisions made by Brussels, Ed Miliband has argued as ministers faced pressure to move further after Friday’s landmark deal with the EU.

Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, said Burnham should push for membership.

“The problem with being outside the bloc is that we end up in a permanent state of negotiation, because we always have to play catchup, rather than having a seat at the table,” she wrote in an article for the Sunday Mirror. “That’s why I think we should simply be back in the European Union.”

Speaking to BBC One’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show, Miliband refused to say whether he now supported discussions on potentially rejoining, but said the deal reached at Friday’s summit – on food and drink, emissions trading and a mutual youth mobility scheme – showed the benefits of closer links, including UK input to EU regulations that were being followed anyway.

“At the moment, what the situation is is that we are essentially rule takers,” the foreign secretary said. “Businesses are rule takers if they want to sell into the European market. So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union, but at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms.”

He said this was “the worst of all worlds” and it meant there was a clear case to integrate more closely into EU markets.

Another reason for even closer ties, he said, was the transformed geopolitical order since 2016, including Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the US’s distancing from Europe under Donald Trump.

He said: “I was not in favour of Brexit, as you know, but I accepted the result, and I think it was right to accept the result. [But] I think there’s a key point: the world has changed massively since 2016, and we can’t stand still.

“How can we say: ‘Well, this is all it is, the status quo is fine, even with the summit today. We’re not even going to look at the future of our relationship with the European Union.’ Of course, we’ve got to do that, and we’ve got to lay out the options.”

Speaking for the Conservatives on the Sunday morning broadcast round, Alex Burghart, Kemi Badenoch’s deputy, said Burnham should simply be concentrating on better defence ties with Europe, arguing that the public would not want to return to the EU.

Asked if the Conservatives would undo the deal made at Friday’s summit if they won power, Burghart said they would. He said: “Yes, we would scrap it. I don’t think that there will be good outcomes from it. And I also don’t think it is a good idea for a country like Britain to hand over control of its rules to another power and have no say over how those rules are created right into the future. This is a silly idea.”

Burnham faces some nervousness in his cabinet and the parliamentary Labour party more widely over talk of possibly rejoining, with some MPs wary about the bitter political fight this could set off.

But Thornberry in her article praised Burnham for having “finally ended the conspiracy of silence over Brexit”, saying polls indicated that a majority of the UK public now backed rejoining.

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-22 11:41 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of the former Prime Minister's perspective on EU plans with clear reporting.

Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'

Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU.

At the Brussels summit this week the PM said he wanted to "brainstorm" options for the future relationship between Britain and the trading bloc.

In an exclusive interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, said: "Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting: "Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer."

May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union.

Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations.

The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019.

Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government.

"It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want.

"And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.

"When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head.

"He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer.

"Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be."

Speaking to the BBC back in 2023, she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union".

Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection.

May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU.

- 'Move on!'

On Saturday, Sir Tony Blair - another former prime minister - weighed in on the UK's future relationship with the EU.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, external, Sir Tony has said Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Sir Tony, a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

It comes after Burnham struck a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday, covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister also said that over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for their long-term relationship.

He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Source: BBC Politics | Published: 2026-11-22 11:50 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Theresa May ‘aghast’ at Andy Burnham’s talk about rejoining EU
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Comprehensive coverage of the former Prime Minister's reaction with useful context and vocabulary.

Theresa May has said she feels “aghast” at Andy Burnham’s plan for potentially rejoining the EU, arguing in a rare interview that the prime minister should “accept Brexit and move on”.

Speaking to the BBC after Friday’s UK-EU summit, at which Burnham secured the biggest step towards renewed ties with Brussels since Brexit, May said that a further move towards membership, as talked about by the PM, would dominate the government’s time.

“What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that had to be put in,” said May, who took over in No 10 from David Cameron shortly after the 2016 referendum and shaped the basics of the very hard departure deal that Boris Johnson eventually sealed.

“It’s across the whole of government. It’s not just prime ministerial time, [it’s] cabinet ministers’ time, officials’ time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations, because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you’re getting out what you want.

“That’s one of the reasons why I looked slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham was talking about – further negotiations of going into the EU. As a country, we voted for Brexit.

“When I was prime minister, I was very clear: we should deliver on that vote. So I’m afraid my message to him really is: people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on.”

May said it was damaging for governments not to trust the results of referendums: “I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people … He wants to pat them on the head and say: ‘You know what? Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come out with the right answer’ – what he thinks is the right answer.”

May’s intervention is an unusual step from the former prime minister, who has typically reserved her public statements since leaving office for areas of cross-party consensus. On taking office, she opted to push for minimal residual ties with the EU as a way to maintain unity in the Conservatives. But she struggled with the Brussels negotiations amid dissent among her MPs, and was ousted in 2019.

Pressed on whether Brexit had been a success, May refused to say, arguing that with global shocks such as Covid and Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine, it was impossible to know.

Asked outright if she believed the UK was in a better or worse state as a result of the decision to leave the EU, she replied: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union.”

The summit in Brussels on Friday saw the announcement of three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.

Burnham, who has condemned the May-Johnson departure deal for hampering growth and gumming up trade, has raised the possibility of even closer ties and that the UK could rejoin the EU in the future.

None of this would happen until after another election, with Burnham committed until then to the Brexit “red lines” of Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which rules out being part of the EU’s customs union or single market.

While the changes in the new deal will be presented to parliament as a bill next week, at the summit, Burnham slightly slowed down the pace of any further moves. He said he would “brainstorm” with the EU over future ties, with the timetable talked about in terms of months, while reiterating that he would not get ahead of public opinion.

The Conservatives have been pushing back against the deal made on Friday, briefing newspapers on Sunday that signing up to the emissions trading system would add costs to domestic energy bills because of EU carbon taxes.

Downing Street argues the deal will bring down energy and food costs, with Burnham saying on Friday it could add as much as 0.5% to GDP in the long term.

item.title: The looming UK winter may spawn a double headache for Andy Burnham | Richard Partington
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed look at the economic challenges facing the Prime Minister with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year with rising inflation.

Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult.

On Wednesday, the regulator Ofgem is expected to confirm a 26% increase in the energy price cap from January, pushing the annual bill to £2,166 for a typical household.

Rising petrol prices and diesel hitting a record high lifted the UK’s headline inflation rate to 3.6% in October, its highest level in a year. The Bank of England says inflation could hit 5% next year.

It is now half a decade since inflation first went above the 2% target set by the government. Consumer prices have galloped by almost a third over that same time. A return to the target is not expected until 2028 at the earliest.

So far, households have proven surprisingly resilient. Consumer confidence surveys bear this out. Retail sales in October were stronger than expected, even though some of this was driven by a rush to stockpile emergency supplies.

But there is a storm coming. Especially if the El Niño forecast is right and we have a very cold January.

As autumn gives way to winter, low-income households will be hardest hit as the mercury drops. Record numbers of families cannot afford the essentials. The places feeling the pinch most will also be the ones where Burnham has promised to turn things around.

Analysis by the Centre for Cities shows that after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, inflation rose most in towns and cities that entered the cost of living crisis in a precarious position. Small towns in the north of England, Midlands and Wales were most exposed. Households in Burnley, Blackburn and Blackpool faced an inflation rate nearly three percentage points higher than those in London, Reading and Cambridge.

Part of this is because the recent inflationary burst has been driven by the price of energy and food, hitting low-income families most because they spend proportionally more on essentials than the wealthiest. And that means some places are harder hit than others because despite the promises of successive governments, Britain’s regional income gaps have barely shifted in three decades.

According to research from the Resolution Foundation, the places that were performing worst in the late 1990s are still at the bottom of the living standards league table a generation later. Disposable incomes in Kensington and Chelsea, at £60,584, remain four-and-a-half times higher than in Leicester, at £13,398.

But in response to the cost of living squeeze, Burnham’s government has, perhaps surprisingly, taken a remarkably blunt approach.

At the autumn budget, the “breathing space” measures announced by John Healey prioritised an across-the-board freeze in fuel duty and £100 energy rebate for every household in council tax bands A to D. The removal of standing charges from gas bills that was also announced will not come into effect until the end of 2027.

The poorest households will benefit from the £150 warm homes discount, on top of a universal VAT cut to electricity bills. But charities warn that overall the government’s limited ambition and relatively poor targeting will fail to meet the moment.

Despite the gloom, there are caveats. After more than three decades of entrenched regional inequality, it would be unreasonable to expect Burnham to turn things around overnight. The legacy of austerity and Britain’s tight fiscal position make his task harder. After years of politicians pursuing a quick fix – often with disastrous consequences – his long-term approach is to be commended.

There are also signs that the outlook could improve. The global oil price has fallen back since the blow to Donald Trump’s authority in the US midterm elections. Brent crude has dropped to about $90 a barrel, down from a peak of close to $120 as recently as the end of October. Growth in Britain’s economy has proven more resilient than feared, helped by the rollout of AI, and unemployment has fallen back in recent months.

Figures show food price inflation was lower than expected in October, at 0.9%, the lowest increase since September 2021. How long this lasts, however, is a moot point, amid expectations of a surge in grocery prices next year linked to higher energy costs and El Niño hitting harvests worldwide.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, suggested last week that the pull back in global energy prices could lead headline inflation to fall short of Threadneedle Street’s forecasts for next year.

However, the longer the Iran war rumbles on, the greater the chance of the Bank raising interest rates to keep inflation in check. Financial markets predict three quarter-point increases next year, adding to the financial squeeze for most households. The first could come as early as next month.

In Britain’s poorest postcodes, a tough winter looms. For Burnham’s No 1 political priority, that is a problem.

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-22 11:24 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: 'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of former Prime Minister's advice with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

"Move on!" That's Theresa May's frank instruction to Andy Burnham.

She spent years wrangling with the EU to try to forge a decent Brexit deal before being shoved out of her job by her party. Her leadership was broken by Britain's relationship with Brussels. Now she is warning the current resident of No 10 not to risk the same.

In a rare interview, Baroness May - who presided over negotiations with the EU between 2016 and 2019 - told me Burnham ought to respect the public's decision 10 years ago, not "pat them on their head" as if they gave the wrong answer and should have "another go".

And she said she was "aghast" at what he was doing, dangling the possibility of rejoining the EU, warning it would absorb huge amounts of government effort.

"The hours that have to be put in, it's across the whole of government," she said. "It's not just prime ministerial time, [it's] cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations."

But while some on his own side are very keen to get on with a campaign to rejoin the EU - and the foreign secretary tells me this option is on the table - May is not the only voice urging caution.

Earlier this month David Cameron also said starting a conversation about rejoining would be "long and painful".

And former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair has told the Sunday Times this weekend that Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

- Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'

- Published2 hours ago

Burnham promised a "brainstorm" on stage in Brussels yesterday, so what's his plan?

The prime minister's precise message on Europe is, maybe characteristically, not that precise.

From the by-election platform in the summer where he promised not to reopen old arguments and emphasised he was not proposing the UK considers rejoining, to telling the BBC the country could "go all the way" and go back in, to now the promises of a "national conversation" and "brainstorm" with the EU - his words have varied over time.

No 10 plainly wants to move closer to the EU, even if ministers suggest there really is no end fixed position and so this period of working it out is genuine.

They tell me that, in private, "Andy is pretty clearly where he is publicly - he does think it's a big discussion we have to have as a country, it's a national discussion in the context of the 10 year plan, but also has to involve the Europeans".

In other words, even though he makes no secret that he'd like to be in the EU and wishes we had never left, the prime minister won't conclude whether he'll promise to take the country back in until he has a better idea of what relationship he might get out of the EU - and, perhaps too, how the public responds.

Two quick reminders: Burnham has said it wouldn't happen before another election; and, remember there are elections in Europe too. This whole conversation might be transformed if Marine Le Pen becomes the president of France, or the march of other parties who are suspicious of Brussels continues.

The prime minister's body language in Brussels yesterday, though, and his proclamation that it was a "good day" for Britain, displays happiness in government at what they have achieved so far - closer ties on food exports, energy, and allowing young people to live and work more freely on both sides of the Channel.

Despite a last minute classic spanner in the works with a lack of agreement on tuition fees, the UK side feels positive they didn't back down on that issue yesterday, and the broader deals were concluded anyway.

And despite the protestations from the foreign secretary that the deals will all come into force whatever happens on fees, the government will start the legal processes to turn the agreements into law - although there are still plenty of opportunities for other countries to try and unpick them further down the track.

Of course, politicians' reactions to the deal depend which side they were on in the Brexit debate.

The Lib Dems, SNP, Greens and Plaid Cymru plead the case that it's not far enough. The Conservatives complain it's not fair, for example, that British farmers will have to follow EU rules to make life easier for those who trade with the bloc. Reform scream it's a betrayal of the 2016 vote.

But the feeling in government is the summit was a success and showed the EU will allow the UK to pick and choose where to cooperate, and is willing to listen to what the prime minister wants to do next. It's worth saying just as in any negotiation, the EU might always be up for giving if it receives in return.

Yet as May warns, doing deals with the European Union is simply, a long hard slog.

And one senior Whitehall source cautions the prime minister not to kid himself that an early feel-good factor doesn't mean future haggling would be a doddle: "British prime ministers can be oddly delusional about the EU - they can get seduced by the hope that good relationships with individual leaders will overcome the ideological inertia in Brussels which is overseen by French and German lawyerly high priests and priestesses.

"European leaders might actually be your friends, but they are not the ones in charge of decision-making in Brussels."

And a former negotiator warns that in his "brainstorm," the prime minister might well find the deal he's concluded this week just about rubs up against the limits of what can be done without going for the full-fat option - telling me: "There isn't much more to go with a strategy of incrementally building on the deal before it becomes quite a binary choice."

They add a reality check for any deal-making with the EU: "The EU have a very set way of doing things, that is more about their own unity than about who they are negotiating with."…

Source: BBC Politics | Published: 2026-11-22 06:01 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100
